userJob: Establish whether this is a block theme or a classic child theme before writing anything
problem: The two kinds of WordPress own layout in different places, so a plan written for one produces edits that the other silently ignores or the site editor overwrites
worksWhen: At stack detection, before the first file is written
avoidWhen: Never; every later decision in this stack forks here
mechanism: A theme.json with a templates directory of HTML files is a block theme and the site editor owns layout. A style.css with a Template header and PHP templates is a classic child theme and PHP owns layout. Write which one into the plan, because token location, route creation and font registration all fork on this answer.
risks: Assuming block theme because the WordPress version is current, when the site runs a classic child
Editing a parent theme or a plugin, which the next update deletes
mobileRules: Block themes carry their own layout and spacing settings that apply at every width; overriding them in a stylesheet reintroduces the mismatch at some breakpoints only
accessibilityRules: Whichever kind it is, the rendered markup is what the accessibility floor is measured against, not the editor's preview
genericnessNote: Identifying the platform variant is a factual step with no design content.

userJob: Put colour, type and spacing values where both the page and the editor can see them
problem: Values are written into a stylesheet, so the site editor keeps offering its own palette and the client meets the mismatch while editing rather than the builder meeting it while building
worksWhen: A block theme, where theme.json compiles settings into custom properties and preset classes
avoidWhen: A classic child theme, which has no such layer and where the stylesheet is the only place values can live
mechanism: Declare colour, typography and spacing under settings in theme.json. WordPress compiles them into preset custom properties and preset classes, in the editor as well as on the page. An important flag aimed at the preset output means the value is in the wrong file.
risks: Two sources of truth for one value, so the editor and the front end disagree and the client sees both
Naming presets generically, which loses the direction's own colour names at exactly the layer the client edits
mobileRules: Spacing and font-size presets can carry fluid values; check the rendered result at 375px rather than trusting the declared range
accessibilityRules: Preset colours appear as editor choices, so any combination the client can pick has to clear contrast, not only the ones you used
genericnessNote: The token layer is where the direction's own names survive into the client's editing experience, and generic names are how a direction quietly reverts.

userJob: Add a page in WordPress without writing to the database from a build step
problem: A route is treated as a file, so a new page is created by adding a template, and the page never exists because the row that would render it does not
worksWhen: Any WordPress build that needs a page the site does not yet have
avoidWhen: The route already exists as content and only its template is being changed
mechanism: A page is a row in the database and the template hierarchy picks what renders it. Block theme: templates and parts as HTML files. Classic child theme: front-page.php and page-slug.php. A new route is new content, so never write to the database from a build step. Report the missing page instead and let it be created as content.
risks: Creating content programmatically during a build, which makes the environment the source of truth instead of the database
Naming a template for a slug that does not exist yet, so the template is dead until someone creates the page
accessibilityRules: Template hierarchy decides which markup renders, so heading structure has to be checked per template rather than once for the theme
genericnessNote: Routing mechanics are factual and carry no design content.

userJob: Load a typeface so the editor and the page both use it
problem: The face is imported from a stylesheet, so it queues behind the CSS and the shift lands after paint, and the editor never sees the face at all
worksWhen: Any WordPress build with a typeface that is not already registered
avoidWhen: The face is already registered by the parent theme or a font plugin the client manages
mechanism: On a block theme, declare the face under fontFamilies with a fontFace entry in theme.json and keep the source inside the theme, so the editor loads it too. On a classic child theme, enqueue it from the child's functions.php on the enqueue hook. Self-host and preload the face used above the fold. Version every enqueued asset from its file modification time.
risks: An optimisation plugin reordering or stripping anything hand-written into a template, which enqueueing avoids and inline tags do not
A font import that loads only on the front end, so the client edits in a different face than they publish
mobileRules: The layout shift from a late face is most visible at 375px where lines rewrap; preload the above-the-fold face rather than all of them
accessibilityRules: Confirm the face carries the weights the scale assumes, since a synthesised weight loses contrast
genericnessNote: Registration is a loading mechanism and does not choose the face.

userJob: Change WooCommerce output without freezing a template at today's version
problem: A plugin template is copied into the child theme and edited, so it stays frozen while the plugin updates around it, and the divergence usually surfaces at checkout
worksWhen: A WooCommerce build where the required change cannot be made through a hook
avoidWhen: The change is appearance only, where an override of cart or checkout is a liability with no upside
mechanism: Prefer a hook. If an override is unavoidable, record the template path and the plugin version it was copied from in the direction record, so a later update can be checked against it. Never override cart or checkout for appearance alone.
risks: An override that renders old markup after an update, discovered by a customer at checkout
Overriding for a change a filter would have made, which trades one line for a permanent maintenance obligation
mobileRules: Checkout at 375px is where a stale override does most damage, because the layout has least room to absorb a markup change
accessibilityRules: A frozen override also freezes whatever accessibility fixes the plugin has shipped since, so the override inherits old defects
genericnessNote: Override discipline is maintenance, not design.

userJob: Diagnose a WordPress change that appears not to have taken effect
problem: A caching plugin serves the previous stylesheet, which reads exactly like a rule that is not applying, and time goes into the CSS instead of into the cache
worksWhen: Any WordPress site with a caching or optimisation plugin, which is most of them
avoidWhen: A local environment with caching disabled, where the symptom means what it looks like
mechanism: Purge the cache before diagnosing a rule that seems not to apply. Separately, block markup edited by hand past its comment delimiters is marked invalid, so the editor discards it the next time the client saves. Both failures are silent and both look like something else.
risks: Adding specificity to defeat a cached stylesheet, which leaves a permanent override once the cache clears
Hand-editing block markup to save a step, which the client's next save quietly undoes
mobileRules: Some optimisation plugins serve different asset bundles by device class, so purge and re-check at 375px separately
accessibilityRules: Discarded block markup takes its heading structure with it, so a page that passed can silently regress after a client edit
genericnessNote: Both are diagnostic facts about the platform.
